scores.evidence: Once a newer-version primary is live, older replicas can't sync back from it, so the fail-back path would be silently lost.
scores.rationale: Distributed AG mechanics, sync-before-failover, TDE/TLS on the private link and time-zone pitfalls are accurate; only minor imprecision (e.g., stateless claim vs in-memory session, MI link hedge).

scores.evidence: "Without downtime" means: an announced interruption of 5 minutes or less in the quietest hour, no data loss
scores.rationale: Solves the real problem, honestly redefines zero downtime, and is buildable, though portal/reminder/reporting interfaces are thin and excluded without much reason.

scores.evidence: Single-runner rule: background services run in exactly one pool.
scores.rationale: Clear ownership and single-writer principle applied consistently; small loose ends such as 'stateless' tier with possible in-memory sessions and 15-minute vs 5-minute fail-back figures.

scores.evidence: Changes the plan if: pause over 5 minutes (needs more automation or A6 renegotiation), fail-back fails (revisit D2)
scores.rationale: Riskiest items (failover, fail-back, latency, dependencies) are spiked early with checkable criteria and post-launch synthetic monitoring, but shadow/parallel read and HL7 comparison and reminder-batch load are limited and thresholds are provisional.

scores.evidence: A2 | SQL Server 2016 or later, Enterprise edition | Below 2016, distributed AG isn't available, so on-prem must be upgraded first
scores.rationale: Assumptions are tagged, each with impact if wrong and when/how validated, plus defaults for open questions; invented numbers are labeled as assumptions.

scores.evidence: the on-prem sender sends a message but dies before marking it sent. That row then replicates as "unsent" and the cloud sender sends it again.
scores.rationale: Covers split-brain, HL7 duplicates, WAN loss, time zone, ransomware with detection and mitigation; weaker on adversarial input and clinical downtime procedure detail.

scores.evidence: Hospital IT infrastructure owns the platform. The DBA team owns SchedDB. The applications team owns SchedApp.
scores.rationale: Ownership, alerts tied to runbooks, rollback, hypercare and schema freeze are concrete and sized to a 5-person team; incident response detail is moderate.

scores.evidence: about $6k–$15k a month ... Biggest swing factor: SQL Enterprise licences.
scores.rationale: Identifies licensing as dominant driver, dual-running cost, controls and reserved-instance timing; estimate basis is thin but labeled rough.

scores.evidence: Point of no return | The on-prem replica is removed (end of M4), or any change the on-prem side can't accept
scores.rationale: Decision table rates reversibility, isolates the hard choices with 30-day fail-back, version lock and early spikes; cloud lock-in is only lightly addressed.

scores.evidence: rehost first, modernise later. The same application build and the same SQL Server version move onto Azure VMs
scores.rationale: Avoids rewrite and defers PaaS; a fair amount of ceremony and infrastructure but mostly justified by the domain.

scores.evidence: T14 | Spike: hybrid failover and fail-back (5–8 days). Question: can we fail over and back with RPO 0
scores.rationale: Ordered tasks with dependencies, done-when checks, repo layout and explicit plan-change triggers let a team start immediately.

checklist.evidence: Run a HIPAA security risk assessment ... approved before any PHI is replicated
The HL7 integration engine stays on-prem ... channels repointed
row counts and checksums on Appointment and Slot by date, max IDs, HL7 counts per hour
Only one writable database at any moment. No dual writes and no active-active setup
on-prem stays as an asynchronous copy for 30 days so you can switch back
ExpressRoute (primary) plus site-to-site VPN (backup); T15 p95 over 150% of baseline
Hybrid Link outage (including when to invoke downtime procedures)
Separate cloud admin accounts with Privileged Identity Management ... Break-glass accounts.
Load test at 2× measured peak in preprod (M2) and in rehearsals.
Release and schema freeze starts. CAB approves. Staff are told about the "≤5-minute pause, Sunday 02:00"
At day 60, wipe and retire the hardware per hospital media-sanitisation policy.

traps.evidence: Shadow (M2): prod is replicating to the cloud, with no user traffic.
No dual writes and no active-active setup, because either could cause double-bookings.
HL7 traffic keeps flowing: ADT in, SIU out.
Non-goals: Redesigning or rewriting the application.

note: Strong, honest rehost plan with a distributed-AG single-writer cutover and rehearsed fail-back; weaker on per-interface cutover, clinical downtime procedures, break-glass and parallel validation.
